name: Adam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your working week look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the brass section of a municipal concert orchestra, write short arrangements for community shows and coach its younger players. I have a master's in music and have held the lead trumpet chair for twenty-seven years. I still like getting a rough rehearsal to breathe together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work support you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my wife works in a pharmacy, and our children have left home. My senior contract pays well, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are several concert groups within a train ride. I use AI now and then for a draft rehearsal schedule, after checking the players' availability myself; I do not feed it their personal records. I want the pension statement in my hands before making any retirement promise.

I'd say **players still listen** together in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players a quicker rehearsal schedule is useful if the contracted playing and arrangement fees remain clear. The band still has to tune and listen in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-month reserve and my wife's wage cover a cancelled concert, while the orchestra remains the main income. I see mild software as an aid to arranging dates, not as a reason to cut a chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll confirm the next season's paid concerts and written arrangement fees. In the first year of mild AI, I'll use only the approved scheduler on dates without personal records, check every booking against the signed rota, and save a fifth of genuinely extra cleared arrangement fees after our bills and instrument upkeep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm while the contract and household pay hold. A neat calendar is not a concert fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks rehearsal dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The librarian sends a list of available rehearsal rooms, but I telephone before a date is fixed. An AI draft cannot know that the trumpet player needs the earlier train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the saving come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifth comes only from extra arrangement money after rent, food and trumpet maintenance, not from a promised fee. An unconfirmed commission contributes nothing to that transfer.

I'd keep **human rehearsal rates** in writing.

Our **live contract** and reserve allow a measured response.

feel: I feel **anxious** about commission income, with live fees still booked.
S1.quote: I will not turn a free trial into an extra unpaid duty.
fieldNote: The **arrangement sixth** of his pay is at risk under moderate AI.
A **paid editing trial** needs approval, licence, privacy and a playable result before use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our manager whether generated arrangements mean fewer paid commissions. I'd want the human rehearsal and playing rates written separately before a cheap score is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short arrangements are about a sixth of my pay. I expect some orders to soften, though the live contract and savings give me time to respond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll total twelve months of arrangement invoices and ask the manager for a written season of live calls. In the first year of this slower change, I'll test an approved AI sketch only if the orchestra pays the editing time, licenses the source and keeps names and unpublished scores out; I will play every line before accepting it, and stop if those terms fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a real slice of my fees. The full live season gives me a way to wait for evidence without pretending a sketch is paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has editing time been paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the manager has not offered paid editing time yet. I will not turn a free trial into an extra unpaid duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a sketch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen a bot put a trumpet phrase beyond a young player's breath. I would correct it at rehearsal or reject the sketch altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band thinking AGI could arrive by 2028, before capable playing robots around 2031. I would ask which concerts and live coaching hours are actually funded now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect arrangement fees to vanish in 2028, taking a sixth of my pay. Live concerts should continue at first, but if their funding also falls I need another paid role rather than a hopeful advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total those fees, seek signed orchestra calls and request an actual pension estimate. In the first year after 2028, if live concert hours also fall, I'll apply only to posted paid brass-coaching jobs that accept my master's and teaching record, with paid in-person brass playing/breathing instruction and written net pay after train fares replacing lost fees and a route I can make; I'll keep current shows until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected sixth disappearing, with nine months saved and other groups nearby. Losing live hours as well would make the situation worse, but I have not assumed that cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a coaching vacancy open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not found a posted coaching vacancy today. A neighbouring music centre is a possibility, not an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you retire on the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A pension estimate might change my choices, but I cannot count on any amount until I see its actual statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra full AGI by 2031 gives us time to price player coaching in the next contract. Playing robots follow around 2034, so I would put the rehearsal ear and safe breathing work in paid human hands before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arrangement fees may dwindle before 2031. I would take a weekly section-coaching hour only if the orchestra funds my instruction and preparation without cutting an existing paid rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next season I'll propose a two-year written section-coaching addendum with paid teaching and preparation, a safe insured room and instruments, and cancellation terms. In the first year after 2031, if arrangement fees end, I'll teach only when a signed hour, actual pupils and safe equipment fit outside booked playing; otherwise I'll keep the contracted chair and refuse to count a phantom coaching wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about arrangement income shrinking before 2031, even with time to bargain. I know how to coach a brass section, but the rate and pupils have to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who provides safe equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra already owns the teaching room and practice horns. Its technician must check the valves and hygiene before an apprentice uses one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the coaching hour signed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one has signed the new coaching hour. I will not ask a pupil to fill a hole in an unsigned budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that full AGI by 2036 lets me read pension figures and written concert dates before deciding when to leave the chair. Playing robots come around 2039, but our bills arrive every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still play at 68. Nine months saved and my wife's pay help, but I cannot decide to retire from a pension number I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year concert plan, then save a fifth of each extra cleared arrangement fee after household bills and horn upkeep toward a year of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid concerts while booked; if arrangement fees stop and the pension estimate still leaves a gap, I'll seek posted paid brass-coaching work only if my master's and teaching qualify, in-person brass playing/breathing instruction is paid, written replacement net after train travel covers lost fees and the route fits, keeping the current chair until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about income that far ahead while present contracts and reserves are sound. I would make a stopping decision only against actual pension and paid-work figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra fee arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no extra arrangement fee, I save nothing from that source. I will not make a savings target a debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know the pension amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the pension office has not sent an estimate yet. My wife and I will read it before I turn down a paid season.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement money could end before I know whether live calls hold. Signed concerts, an actual pension estimate and a posted coaching role with written travel-adjusted pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays a senior player to listen to a beginner breathe. A good brass lesson needs a booked hour, not a compliment.

headlineQuote: A good brass lesson needs a booked hour, not a compliment.
portrait: Adam is a **58-year-old senior trumpet lead** with a master's degree, partner and grown children.
His **higher contract pay**, partner wage and nine-month reserve support a measured search among nearby groups.
He **occasionally uses AI** for nameless date drafts and verifies bookings himself.
He requires **signed paid coaching** before treating apprentice hours as replacement income.
biggestWorry: **2028 thinking AGI** could end arrangement fees worth one sixth of Adam’s own pay before live funding is clear.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed concert calls**, an actual pension estimate and posted qualifying paid brass coaching with replacement net after travel would help.
